title: SYSK’s Summer Movie Playlist: Why was Titicut Follies banned?
summary: Chuck and Josh discuss the 1967 documentary Titicut Follies by Frederick Wiseman, shot at Bridgewater State Hospital in Massachusetts. They cover cinema verite filmmaking, the history of Bridgewater from an 1854 poorhouse to a hospital for the criminally insane, civil commitment, specific disturbing scenes (the guards taunting Jim, the force feeding, Vladimir's appeal), and the decades-long legal battle over privacy that banned the film until a 1991 ruling lifted restrictions. The episode also includes a listener mail segment about effective altruism and a brief banter opening. This is a Summer Movie Playlist episode, presented by Chuck as a re-airing.

segments.title: Episode introduction
segments.summary: Chuck introduces the Summer Movie Playlist episode on Titicut Follies, calling it a serious film and a rerun-style re-airing.

segments.title: Opening banter
segments.summary: Hosts joke about Jerry's vacation and chat about Kevin Pollock, Better Things, and Project Greenlight.

segments.title: Introducing Titicut Follies and Frederick Wiseman
segments.summary: The hosts introduce Titicut Follies as a notorious documentary by Frederick Wiseman, a former law professor, about a Massachusetts institution for the criminally insane. They note its reputation for disturbing content and that it was banned in places, though it is a straightforward cinema verite film.

segments.title: Cinema verite explained
segments.summary: Hosts define cinema verite, or direct cinema, as filming life without interviews or staging, and discuss Wiseman's view that people act like themselves on camera.

segments.title: Early cinema verite and documentary style
segments.summary: Discussion of Richard Leacock and Robert Drew's Mooney Versus Fowl, Drew's view of documentary as journalism, and debate about recreations in documentaries such as The Kid Stays in the Picture and Forensic Files.
topics: The Kid Stays in the Picture

segments.title: History of Bridgewater State Hospital
segments.summary: Bridgewater began in 1854 as a Massachusetts poorhouse, later took in criminals and the mentally ill, became the State Asylum for Insane Criminals in 1895, and was transferred to the Massachusetts Bureau of Prisons. Its population included violent criminals alongside people held for minor offenses.

segments.title: Civil commitment and a case of long confinement
segments.summary: Hosts describe civil commitment and how people could be held for years without medical review. They recount a man arrested in 1927 for stealing groceries who spent 28 years at Bridgewater before release in 1963.

segments.title: Wiseman's background
segments.summary: Hosts begin Wiseman's biography: he attended Yale law school, was drafted for the Korean War, lived in Paris with his wife Zorita Batshaw, and became interested in filmmaking as cinema verite developed in France.

segments.title: Wiseman's path to filmmaking and making the film
segments.summary: Wiseman returned to Boston and taught law at BU, produced The Cool World, directed by Shirley Clarke, and took law classes to Bridgewater. He obtained permission from state officials and filmed for 29 days, shooting many hours of footage before editing to 83 minutes. The title refers to a Native American name for the area.

segments.title: Opening scenes and YouTube viewing
segments.summary: The film opens with an inmate musical performance of Strike Up the Band. Wiseman guards his films closely, so clips are hard to find legally, and the hosts discuss a pirated VHS copy online.

segments.title: The shaving scene and guards taunting Jim
segments.summary: Hosts describe a fast shaving scene and the guards who repeatedly taunt a patient named Jim about his room, which is empty and where he is kept naked, until he reacts.

segments.title: Wiseman's neutrality and staff portrayal
segments.summary: Hosts discuss how Wiseman shows staff and patients with equal treatment, without a narrator or music, including a patient who describes abusing children.

segments.title: Ambient sound and available light in cinema verite
segments.summary: Hosts compare the film's lack of artificial score and lighting with a Cleveland Indians throwback game. They discuss how the film keeps real background noise and available light, making the viewer feel like a witness.

segments.title: Vladimir's parole pleas and medication
segments.summary: Hosts describe Vladimir, a lucid patient who asks to return to prison, complains about noisy TVs and medication, and is later discussed by staff as paranoid.

segments.title: Lack of narration and the force-feeding scene
segments.summary: Hosts note that the film has no captions or explanations of who the patients are. They discuss a force-feeding scene that Wiseman later called ham-fisted, intercut with a burial preparation.

segments.title: Editing and manipulation
segments.summary: Chuck and Josh discuss how Wiseman said he manipulates viewers through editing and disliked the term cinema verite, and how this was his first film.

segments.title: Wiseman's permissions and the film's initial reception
segments.summary: Wiseman obtained written and on-camera permission from officials and those filmed. Officials including the superintendent and Lieutenant Governor reportedly liked the film initially, but after release to wider audiences the response turned negative.

segments.title: Ban and privacy court case
segments.summary: Elliott Richardson, who had higher political aspirations, sought to suppress the film and accused Wiseman of double-crossing the state. Judge Harry Cowin ruled in 1968 that the film breached privacy and ordered the negative destroyed, leading to an appeal that established a right to privacy in Massachusetts. The ACLU proposed limited screening for professionals.

segments.title: Limited screenings, lawsuits, and the 1991 unbanning
segments.summary: The film was shown in film classes, medical schools, and libraries. In the 1980s, class action suits linked suicides at Bridgewater to the film being hidden. A later judge required face blurring, which Wiseman refused, and in 1991 Justice Andrew Meyer's court allowed unrestricted showing since no inmate or family had objected.

segments.title: Distribution, Bridgewater today, and Wiseman's career
segments.summary: PBS aired the film in 1993 and it is available on Canopy through library cards. Hosts note ongoing Bridgewater issues, including chemical restraints, and Wiseman's body of 48 films, including City Hall (2020). Wiseman's wife Zipporah Films is named after her.

segments.title: Listener mail on effective altruism
segments.summary: A listener from Giving What We Can, Grace Adams, wrote in to praise the earlier effective altruism episode and offer free books. Toby Ord also sent well wishes.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Hosts sign off, direct listeners to a free book offer and to contact the show by email.
